terms.gloss: to be to blame, be at fault
terms.grammar: phrase: in + ablative of culpa, with esse
evidence: Ter. Hec. 4.4.78: is quidem in culpā nōn est (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The plain way to say who is to blame. Turned round, mea culpa est is “it’s my fault” (Cic. Brut. 133).

evidence: Liv. 35.33.3: penes Aetōlōs culpam bellī esse (Lewis & Short, s.v. culpa)
Ter. Hec. 4.1.20: culpa, quae tē est penes

terms.gloss: it is someone’s doing (that something did not happen)
terms.grammar: phrase: per + accusative, mostly with quōminus or nē
evidence: Quint. 3.6.78: nōn per mē stetit, sed per illud (Lewis & Short, s.v. stō)
terms.comment: Used of a hindrance: per eum stetit quōminus …, “it was his fault that … did not happen”. Rarely without a negative.

terms.gloss: the person who caused something, the one behind it
evidence: Sall. J. 1.4: suam quisque culpam auctōrēs ad negōtia trānsferunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Not only an author: whoever brings a thing about, for good or ill, so the doer or instigator of an act; also of a woman (Lewis & Short, “comm.”). It names the person, not the fault.

phrases.latin: Stultum est querī dē adversīs, ubi culpa est tua.
phrases.english: It’s foolish to complain of bad luck when the fault is your own.

phrases.latin: mālō Tīrōnis verēcundiam in culpā esse quam inlīberālitātem Curiī
phrases.english: I would rather Tiro’s shyness were to blame than Curius’s meanness

phrases.latin: Nōn est in culpā canis; ego jānuam apertam relīquī.
phrases.english: The dog isn’t to blame; I left the door open.
